learning_goals: Explain what a large language model (LLM) is and its main limits
Describe what RAG stands for and the meaning of each word
List the three steps that happen when a question is answered with RAG
Identify one benefit and one limitation of using RAG

analogy.story: Imagine a student sitting for an open‑book exam in a Hindi‑medium school. The student first looks through the textbook to find the page that has the needed formula, then writes the answer using that page.
analogy.mapping: Looking for the right page = retrieval (finding the relevant chunk). Writing the answer from that page = generation (the LLM produces the final answer).

worked_example.setting: A first‑year college student in Bhopal uses a chatbot on the college website to ask about the new merit‑scholarship rules.
worked_example.question: What is the income limit for the merit scholarship this year?
documents: Scholarship Notice 2024: Family annual income must not exceed ₹2,50,000 for merit scholarship eligibility.
Hostel Fee Circular 2023: Hostel fees are ₹12,000 per semester for all students.
Exam Schedule 2024: Semester exams start on 15 November 2024.
worked_example.retrieved: Scholarship Notice 2024: Family annual income must not exceed ₹2,50,000 for merit scholarship eligibility.
worked_example.answer_without_rag: The income limit is ₹3,00,000 per year. (This is made up; the model guessed.)
worked_example.answer_with_rag: According to the 2024 scholarship notice, the family annual income must not exceed ₹2,50,000.

sections.heading: ## What You Will Learn
sections.goal: Give the learner a clear list of the lesson outcomes.
points: Understand what a large language model (LLM) is and its limits (F1‑F4).
Learn the full form of RAG and the meaning of each word (F5).
See the three question‑time steps: retrieve, augment, generate (F8).
Know one benefit and one limitation of RAG (F11‑F12).

sections.heading: ## Before We Start: Some Basic Ideas
sections.goal: Introduce AI, LLM, token, training data, knowledge cutoff, hallucination.
points: A large language model (LLM) is an AI model trained on a very large amount of text (F1).
It predicts the next token (a word or part of a word) to generate text (F1).
Its knowledge comes from training data that stops at a fixed date called the knowledge cutoff (F2).
It does not know private or organisation‑specific information it never saw (F3).
It can produce confident but wrong answers; this is called hallucination (F4).

sections.heading: ## What Is RAG?
sections.goal: Define RAG and explain each word.
points: RAG stands for Retrieval‑Augmented Generation (F5).
Retrieval = finding the relevant pieces of information from an outside source (F5).
Augmented = adding those pieces to the user question inside the prompt (F5).
Generation = the LLM writes the answer using the question plus the added information (F5).
The term was introduced in a 2020 research paper by Patrick Lewis and colleagues (F6).

sections.heading: ## Why Does RAG Matter?
sections.goal: Show benefits and why we use RAG instead of retraining.
points: Answers can use up‑to‑date and private information (F11).
Fewer made‑up answers (hallucinations are reduced, not removed) (F11).
Answers can show their sources (F11).
Cheaper and faster than retraining the model (F11).
Knowledge is easy to update by changing the documents, not the model (F9, F10).
RAG does not change the model weights; fine‑tuning does (F9, F10).

sections.heading: ## How Does RAG Work?
sections.goal: Explain preparation (indexing) and the three question‑time steps.
points: Preparation (indexing): collect documents, split them into small pieces called chunks (F7).
Each chunk is turned into an embedding (a list of numbers that captures meaning) using an embedding model (F7).
Embeddings are stored in a vector database so they can be searched by meaning (F7).
Question‑time step 1 – Retrieve: the user question is also turned into an embedding; the system finds the most similar chunks using semantic search (F8).
Question‑time step 2 – Augment: the retrieved chunks are placed into the prompt together with the question and an instruction such as "answer using only this information" (F8).
Question‑time step 3 – Generate: the LLM writes the answer from the question plus the retrieved context and can cite the sources (F8).
Only the top few (top‑k) chunks are used; the LLM does not read every document (F8, M5).

sections.heading: ## Example: College Scholarship Chatbot
sections.goal: Walk through the worked example with Indian context.
points: Setting: a student in Bhopal asks the college chatbot about the merit‑scholarship income limit.
The knowledge base holds three short documents (see worked_example.documents).
Retrieval finds the scholarship notice chunk (worked_example.retrieved).
Without RAG the LLM guesses ₹3,00,000 (worked_example.answer_without_rag).
With RAG the answer quotes the correct limit ₹2,50,000 (worked_example.answer_with_rag).

sections.heading: ## Key Words to Remember
sections.goal: List the most important terms with one‑sentence definitions.
points: large language model (LLM) – an AI model trained on huge text that predicts the next token.
token – a word or part of a word that the model reads or writes.
training data – the text collection used to teach the model.
knowledge cutoff – the date after which the model knows nothing.
hallucination – a confident but wrong answer made up by the model.
retrieval – finding the most relevant document pieces for a question.
augmented – adding those pieces to the prompt.
generation – the model writing the final answer.
embedding – a list of numbers that represents the meaning of text.
vector database – a searchable store of embeddings.
semantic search – searching by meaning, not just keywords.
prompt – the full text sent to the model, including question and context.
context – the retrieved chunks placed in the prompt.
fine‑tuning – extra training that changes the model weights.
weights – the internal numbers the model learns during training.
retraining – teaching the model again from scratch or on new data.

sections.heading: ## Quick Check
sections.goal: Five simple questions to test understanding.
points: What does RAG stand for? – Retrieval‑Augmented Generation.
Which step happens first when a question arrives: retrieve, augment, or generate? – Retrieve.
Does RAG change the model’s weights? – No, the weights stay the same.
What is one benefit of RAG? – It lets the model use fresh or private documents.
What is one limitation of RAG? – The answer is only as good as the chunks that are retrieved.

sections.heading: ## Summary
sections.goal: Recap the whole lesson in a few sentences.
points: A large language model (LLM) generates text but has a knowledge cutoff, no private data, and can hallucinate.
RAG (Retrieval‑Augmented Generation) adds a retrieval step before generation so the model answers from up‑to‑date or private documents.
Documents are split into chunks, turned into embeddings, and stored in a vector database.
At question time the system retrieves the best chunks, augments the prompt, and the LLM generates a grounded answer.
RAG is cheaper and faster than retraining, but its quality depends on the retrieved chunks.

quiz.q: What is the full form of RAG?
In RAG, which step comes first when a user asks a question?
Does RAG modify the model’s internal weights?
quiz.a: No, RAG does not change the model weights.

quiz.q: Give one advantage of using RAG over fine‑tuning.
quiz.a: RAG is cheaper and faster and lets you update knowledge by changing documents.

quiz.q: What is a key limitation of RAG?
quiz.a: The answer quality depends on the relevance and correctness of the retrieved chunks.
